title: Ephemeral routing shards for zero-tail-latency upgrades
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Upgrades of Dedicated fleet hosts currently cause small but measurable tail-latency spikes during connection handoffs and cache rehoming. Existing rolling upgrade strategies reduce average disruption but still surface transient token-level latency deviations that affect latency-sensitive customers with tight throughput contracts.

Proposal: Implement an "ephemeral routing shard" mechanism in the control plane that creates short-lived routing islands (micro-shards) which absorb a bounded fraction of traffic and act as migration brokers. Each ephemeral shard: 1) reserves a tokenized throughput contract slice, 2) maintains affinity to a warm micro-pool on target hosts, and 3) performs progressive state rehoming (KV prefetch, prefix warm-up) while enforcing per-shard latency budgets. This approach isolates tail events into tiny shards, allowing upgrades to proceed without perturbing the majority of traffic and without requiring full fleet standby capacity.

Goals:
- Eliminate >=95th-percentile tail spikes during host upgrades for pinned customers with throughput guarantees.
- Keep additional reserve capacity usage <5% of fleet for steady-state maintenance.
- Provide an operator-facing safety knob to pause shard creation or increase shard isolation for high-risk upgrades.
acceptance_criteria: Control plane can create ephemeral routing shards and attach a throughput reservation token to each
Shard routing enforces a max traffic slice per shard and respects global quota guards
Shard-level telemetry surfaced in Console: per-shard latency percentiles, reserved vs observed throughput, and warmup progress
Upgrade campaign with shards shows no >5% increase in 99th percentile latency across 3 test fleets compared to baseline
Automated rollback triggers if shard warmup fails or tail metrics exceed configured thresholds
implementation_notes: Shard lifecycle managed by maintenance orchestrator subcontroller (new microservice) that speaks with router and autoscaler APIs
Throughput reservation implemented as token-bucket lease attached to shard identifier; tokens decrement as requests are routed
Warm micro-pools are small, short-lived allocations on target hosts with pre-seeded KV caches and an isolated batching lane
Routing changes are sticky per-request via route headers to avoid cross-shard interference; we reuse existing affinity headers to minimize client changes
Fallback policy: requests in a failing shard are transparently rerouted to a compatible fallback model variant with graceful degradation and cost accounting
risks_and_tradeoffs: Extra control-plane complexity: new orchestration state machine adds operational load and requires strong observability
Small reserve capacity consumption increases cost; must tune shard size and lifetime to balance risk vs spend
Edge cases where affinity breaks (long-lived sessions) could cause request migrations that are expensive to repair; mitigation: session pinning TTL + proactive migration hooks
Caching semantics: some models may not warm effectively in micro-pools, leading to reduced per-request efficiency during shard lifetime
rollout_plan: Prototype: single-region test cluster, synthetic traffic harness that mimics a heavy-embedding workload (2/ week)
Canary: enable shards for 0.5% of production traffic on low-risk customers with non-critical SLAs (2 cycles)
Golden: expand to 5% with telemetry thresholds and automated rollback alerts (1 cycle)
GA: enable for all maintenance windows, opt-in toggle for customers to request shard-based upgrades via Console
monitoring_and_alerts: ShardWarmupProgress stalls > 5m -> SRE runbook page and channel alert
ReservedTokenUtilization > 90% for 10m -> autoscaler consideration and operator notification
ShardLeak (shard not destroyed within TTL + 1m) -> automatic quiesce and release workflow
testing_plan: Unit tests for shard lifecycle state transitions
Integration tests: router + shard controller + autoscaler in local cluster
Load tests: 99th/99.9th percentile latency under simulated upgrades using k6 harness
Chaos tests: introduce host slowdowns to validate fallback policies and rollback
